what_its_for: Nusinersen is used to treat spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), a rare genetic disease that weakens the muscles and makes it hard to move, breathe, and swallow. It works by helping your body make more of a protein called SMN, which is needed to keep nerve cells healthy and allow muscles to work properly.
how_to_take: Nusinersen is NOT a pill or injection you give yourself at home. It is given by a trained healthcare provider as an injection directly into the fluid surrounding your spinal cord. This is called an intrathecal injection or spinal injection. You will receive this treatment at a hospital, clinic, or specialized medical center. Each injection visit usually takes a few hours, and you may need to lie flat for a period of time after the injection. Your care team will walk you through exactly what to expect before, during, and after each visit.
dosing: The usual dosing schedule works like this: You will receive 4 starting doses called 'loading doses.' These are given on Day 1, Day 15, Day 29, and Day 64. After those first 4 doses, you will receive 1 maintenance dose every 4 months for the rest of your life, as long as your doctor feels it is helping you. Your doctor may adjust this schedule based on your needs, so always follow the plan your care team sets for you.
missed_dose: Because this medication is given by a healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital, it is very important to keep all of your scheduled appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or care team right away so they can set up a new time as soon as possible. Do not skip doses without talking to your doctor, as staying on schedule is important for the medicine to work as well as possible.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. Nusinersen is stored and handled entirely by the healthcare team at the clinic or hospital where you receive your injections. If you are ever given any supplies related to your treatment to take home, ask your care team for specific storage instructions.
what_to_avoid: There are no major food or drink restrictions known with nusinersen. However, you should always tell your doctor and care team about ALL medicines, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you take, because some medications may affect how nusinersen works or increase the risk of side effects. Avoid skipping your scheduled injection appointments, as regular dosing is key to keeping the medicine effective.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the nearest emergency room right away if you notice any of the following after your injection: severe headache that does not go away or gets worse when you sit or stand up (this could be a sign of low spinal fluid pressure), back pain, neck pain, or stiffness that is new or getting worse, signs of infection such as fever, chills, redness, or swelling near the injection site, unusual bruising or bleeding such as blood in your urine, bloody stools, or coughing up blood, swelling in your legs or feet, sudden decrease in how much urine you are making, or any new or worsening weakness, numbness, or changes in how you feel. Also contact your doctor if you think you have missed a dose or need to reschedule an appointment.
when_it_works: Nusinersen may not produce changes right away. Improvements in muscle strength and motor skills may develop slowly over weeks to months. Some patients, especially infants treated early in life before symptoms appear, may show better results than those treated later. Every patient responds differently. It is important to keep all of your appointments and continue treatment even if you do not notice immediate changes. Your doctor will check your progress regularly using physical exams and other tests.
special_populations: Children and Infants: Nusinersen is approved for use in patients of all ages, including newborns. Early treatment, before symptoms develop, tends to produce the best results. Parents and caregivers should work closely with a pediatric neuromuscular specialist. Pregnant or Breastfeeding Women: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. There is limited information about nusinersen use during pregnancy and breastfeeding, so your doctor will help you weigh the risks and benefits. Kidney or Liver Problems: Nusinersen is not processed through the kidneys or liver in the usual way, but let your doctor know about any kidney or liver conditions you have, as they will monitor you closely.
